title: AI Governance for Boards
summary: A ten-module programme giving boards and directors the understanding and tools to govern AI responsibly and evidence sound oversight to regulators.
intro: This training programme equips boards and directors with the understanding and tools to govern AI responsibly: setting risk appetite, challenging management and evidencing sound oversight to regulators.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give directors a practical, jargon-free grounding in how AI is used in financial services and the risks it brings, with the governance tools to oversee it. Participants leave able to set the board's expectations, challenge management and the control functions, and evidence effective oversight to regulators and auditors.
sections.What It Covers: AI strategy and risk appetite, governance and accountability, model risk and explainability, fairness and customer outcomes, AI in trading and advice, resilience and third-party risk, AI regulation across jurisdictions, board reporting and assurance, and the board's own capability.
Intended Audience: Chairs, non-executive and independent directors and board committee members, especially on risk, audit and technology committees
Executive directors and senior managers accountable for AI, risk and compliance
Company secretaries and heads of governance supporting board oversight
Learning Objectives: Explain in plain language how AI works, where the firm uses it and what can go wrong
Define the board's AI accountabilities and evaluate the firm's governance framework
Challenge AI strategy and set a risk appetite with measurable limits
Oversee model risk, fairness and customer outcomes using structured board-level questions
Assess resilience, third-party and regulatory risk, including emerging AI regulation
Specify the information and assurance the board needs, and agree an action plan
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about two hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a two- to three-day programme or as a series of board briefing sessions. Each module combines a short briefing with case studies and a board question set, and modules can be selected or tailored to the board's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Board or senior management experience in financial services is helpful. No technical background in AI or data science is required.
Core Reading: OECD, Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (2019, revised 2024)
NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) (2023)
FSB, The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence (2024)

modules.title: Artificial Intelligence for Directors
modules.summary: Plain-language grounding in how machine learning and generative AI are built and deployed, how they differ from rules-based tools, and why they change the firm's risk profile.
objectives: Explain how AI systems learn, decide and fail
Distinguish machine learning, generative AI and traditional models, and their risks
Identify where AI is already embedded in the firm, including through vendors
syllabus: How AI works: data, training, testing and deployment
Machine learning versus generative AI and large language models
Build versus buy: accountability for third-party AI
The vocabulary directors need: drift, bias, hallucination, explainability

modules.title: Board Accountability and AI Governance Structures
modules.summary: Where accountability for AI sits, what a sound governance framework looks like, and how oversight is divided between the board, its committees and management.
objectives: Define the board's responsibilities for AI and distinguish them from management's
Evaluate the firm's AI governance framework, policies and model inventory
Allocate oversight across committees and the three lines of defence
syllabus: Directors' duties and senior executive accountability for AI-driven decisions
Elements of a governance framework: policy, inventory, ownership and escalation
Committee mandates: board, risk, audit and technology
Common governance failures and their consequences

modules.title: AI Strategy, Risk Appetite and Value
modules.summary: How boards decide where AI should and should not be used, test management's business cases, and set a risk appetite that balances innovation against conduct, prudential and operational risk.
objectives: Challenge management's AI strategy and claimed benefits
Set an AI risk appetite with measurable limits and escalation triggers
Weigh innovation against conduct, prudential and operational risk
syllabus: Questions to ask of an AI strategy: purpose, benefit, cost, dependency and exit
Drafting a risk appetite statement: in-scope uses, prohibited uses and limits
Avoiding hype and paralysis: pilots and staged adoption
Investment, capability and talent decisions for board approval

modules.title: Model Risk, Explainability and Board Challenge
modules.summary: How to oversee model risk for machine learning and generative AI, what explainability can realistically deliver, and the questions the board should put to management and model validators.
objectives: Explain why complex and generative models carry greater model risk
Assess model documentation, validation and monitoring standards
Use a structured question set to probe model risk assurance
syllabus: Opacity, drift and over-reliance in complex models
Explainability by use case, from credit decisions to trading
Good practice in documentation, independent validation and monitoring
A board question set for approving, extending or retiring a model

modules.title: Fairness, Conduct and Consumer Outcomes
modules.summary: The board's responsibility for fair outcomes where AI makes or influences decisions: how bias arises, how fairness is tested, and how the board gains assurance on customer treatment.
objectives: Explain how bias and proxy discrimination enter AI-driven decisions
Evaluate whether bias testing and outcome monitoring give real assurance
Identify the conduct, legal and reputational exposure of unfair outcomes
syllabus: Sources of bias: historical data, proxies and feedback loops
Fairness measures in credit, insurance pricing and targeting
Consumer protection, fair treatment and non-discrimination obligations applied to AI
Case studies of AI bias harms and remediation

modules.title: AI in Trading, Advice and Client Services
modules.summary: The business-line uses of AI with the greatest conduct and market integrity risk, and the controls, kill-switches and escalation arrangements the board should expect.
objectives: Explain how AI is used in trading, investment and client-facing advice
Assess market integrity, suitability and mis-selling risks
Judge the adequacy of controls, human oversight and escalation protocols
syllabus: Algorithmic trading, portfolio construction and signal generation
Market integrity risks: correlated behaviour and flash events
Robo-advice, chatbots and the guidance versus advice boundary
Kill-switches and escalation: what the board should require

modules.title: Operational Resilience, Cyber and Third-Party AI Risk
modules.summary: How AI systems fail and can be attacked, how reliance on a few AI vendors concentrates risk, and whether the firm can withstand and recover from an AI failure.
objectives: Recognise how AI fails, including drift, data poisoning and prompt injection
Assess concentration and dependency on third-party AI providers
Evaluate resilience testing and incident escalation to the board
syllabus: Drift, silent degradation and late detection of AI problems
Adversarial attacks and the board's cyber oversight role
Vendor and foundation-model dependency: due diligence and exit planning
Operational resilience and outsourcing expectations applied to AI

modules.title: AI Regulation and Regulatory Expectations of Boards
modules.summary: The legal and regulatory obligations AI creates for the firm and the board: how jurisdictions are regulating AI, how this overlays existing financial services rules, and what supervisors and auditors expect to see.
objectives: Explain the main approaches to AI regulation and the duties they place on firms
Identify which of the firm's AI uses are likely to be treated as high-risk and the assurance they require
Prepare the board to evidence oversight to supervisors and auditors
syllabus: Approaches to AI regulation across jurisdictions: risk-based laws, sectoral rules, supervisory guidance and managing divergence
International standards and frameworks, including OECD, NIST, ISO/IEC 42001, IOSCO, FSB and BIS
Interaction with existing conduct, prudential, consumer protection and data protection rules
Preparing for supervisory engagement: what the board should be able to show

modules.title: Board Reporting, Management Information and Assurance
modules.summary: The information boards need to oversee AI, how to read dashboards and incident reports critically, and how to obtain credible independent assurance rather than relying on assertion.
objectives: Specify the management information and indicators the board needs
Interpret AI reports and identify what is missing
Obtain independent assurance from internal audit and external reviewers
syllabus: The core board information set: inventory, risk ratings, incidents and outcomes
Key risk indicators and early warning measures
Recognising comfort without evidence
Internal audit, external validation and regulatory reviews as assurance

modules.title: Leading AI Oversight: Capability, Culture and Emerging Risks
modules.summary: Brings the programme together into a board action plan covering the board's own capability, culture, emerging risks from generative AI and agents, and keeping governance current.
objectives: Assess the board's AI literacy and plan to close gaps
Anticipate governance issues from generative AI and autonomous agents
Produce a board action plan for AI oversight
syllabus: Board skills, external advice and how much expertise is enough
Culture and speaking up on AI concerns
Generative AI and autonomous agents: accountability and control questions
Workshop: the board's twelve-month AI oversight plan

related.title: Board Effectiveness: Dynamics and Decision-Making
related.summary: A ten-module programme helping boards strengthen their dynamics, information and decision-making, and evidence effective oversight to supervisors.

related.title: Climate and Sustainability for Boards
related.summary: An eight-module programme giving boards and directors the understanding and tools to oversee climate and nature-related risk, transition plans and sustainability disclosures.

related.title: Culture, Conduct and Accountability for Boards
related.summary: An eight-module programme giving boards the tools to shape and oversee culture, align incentives, hold individuals to account and evidence oversight to regulators.

related.title: Effective Governance for Boards and Directors
related.summary: A twelve-module programme covering the standards expected of individual directors and the practices that make a board effective, for regulated firms, fund boards and management companies.

related.title: Finance and Prudential Essentials for Directors of Regulated Firms
related.summary: An eight-module programme giving non-financial directors the confidence to read a regulated firm's accounts, capital and liquidity position, and to challenge the CFO.

related.title: Financial Crime Oversight for Boards
related.summary: An eight-module programme giving boards the understanding and tools to oversee financial crime risk and evidence effective oversight to supervisors.
